splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate an employer's withdrawal liability from a multiemployer pension plan to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year, or whether the actuary may adopt assumptions after that date. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers in multiemployer plans.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions must be selected before or by the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), providing employers with greater predictability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuaries may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be fixed by that date.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the court-ordered supervision period beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects revocation proceedings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Supervised release is tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that the supervised release term is tolled while a supervisee is a fugitive, so the clock does not run during the period of absconding.

positions.label: Supervised release is not tolled during absconding
positions.summary: Holds that without explicit statutory authorization, courts cannot toll the supervised release term when a supervisee absconds, and the term continues to run.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prevents relitigating claims already presented in a prior habeas petition — applies to federal prisoners bringing successive § 2255 motions. If it applies, federal prisoners face a stricter gatekeeping requirement than Congress may have intended, as they would be barred from raising any previously presented claim regardless of merit.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, categorically preventing them from relitigating any claim already presented.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions; instead, such prisoners need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagreed on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules like ballot-receipt deadlines. The question affects whether election-administration challenges can be brought before elections or must wait until after, with significant implications for mail-in voting procedures nationwide.

positions.label: Candidate has standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates suffer a cognizable competitive injury from state election laws that allegedly dilute or affect the counting of lawful votes, sufficient to confer Article III standing for pre-election challenges.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

positions.label: Candidate lacks standing
positions.summary: Holds that a candidate's generalized competitive concerns about election rules do not establish a concrete, particularized injury sufficient for Article III standing absent a showing of specific harm.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Jacobson v. Florida Secretary of State

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations (Auer/Kisor deference) when construing ambiguous criminal sentencing provisions.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether lenity trumps deference to the Sentencing Commission's commentary when interpreting ambiguous Guidelines provisions in criminal cases. The Third Circuit held that deference can override lenity, placing it at odds with the Fourth, Fifth, and Eleventh Circuits, which hold that lenity prevails. The issue has taken on new significance after Loper Bright overruled Chevron.

positions.label: Lenity trumps agency/Commission deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity is a traditional canon of construction that takes priority over deference to agency or Sentencing Commission interpretations, particularly in criminal or quasi-criminal contexts.

positions.label: Deference can trump lenity
positions.summary: Holds that Auer/Kisor deference to agency or Sentencing Commission commentary can override the rule of lenity when the commentary reasonably interprets ambiguous provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy, is a valid and authoritative interpretation of the Guidelines text after Kisor v. Wilkie.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Sentencing Commission's commentary adding inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) to the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' is entitled to deference, given that the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses. The split affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy convictions can be sentenced as career offenders.

positions.label: Commentary is authoritative — inchoate offenses qualify
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the ambiguous guideline text, and inchoate offenses like conspiracy qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary is invalid — inchoate offenses do not qualify
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and the commentary impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, especially after Kisor narrowed deference principles.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in the safety-valve provision means a defendant must meet all three listed criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any single criterion is disqualifying. The split creates disparate sentencing outcomes for defendants with identical criminal histories depending on the circuit in which they are sentenced.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria must be met to disqualify
positions.summary: Holds that 'and' means 'and,' so a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are satisfied.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that meeting any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement in U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) authorizing such consideration exceeds the Commission's authority.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can be considered as extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. The Seventh and Eighth Circuits have held such changes cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons, while other circuits have permitted consideration of non-retroactive changes as part of the totality of circumstances. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this but has itself become a source of further disagreement.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot, alone or in combination with other factors, constitute an extraordinary and compelling reason for sentence reduction under § 3582(c)(1)(A).

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law may be considered, at least in combination with other factors, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose punishment for the underlying conduct that violated conditions of supervised release when revoking supervised release, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: The Sixth Circuit allows district courts to expressly punish defendants for the conduct underlying their supervised release violations, placing it at odds with circuits that hold revocation sentences must be based on the breach of trust (the violation of the supervisory relationship), not punishment for the new conduct. The Sixth Circuit's internal dissents have flagged this as creating an extreme position in a circuit split.

positions.label: Courts may punish for underlying violation conduct
positions.summary: Holds that courts may consider and impose sentences based on the severity of the underlying criminal conduct that violated the conditions of supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation sentences address breach of trust, not punishment for conduct
positions.summary: Holds that the purpose of a revocation sentence is to sanction the defendant's breach of the court's trust inherent in the supervisory relationship, rather than to punish for the new criminal conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a prior state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state statute covers substances not listed on federal drug schedules.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' in § 4B1.2(b) requires the substance at issue to be federally controlled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally scheduled.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — any state drug offense qualifies
positions.summary: Holds that § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include state law offenses regardless of whether the substance is controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Substance must be federally controlled
positions.summary: Holds that for a prior state conviction to qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines, the substance must also be controlled under federal law.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners challenging the conditions or execution of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration of confinement) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring claims under Bivens or other civil-rights statutes.
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for challenges to conditions of confinement that affect the execution of a sentence (e.g., BOP decisions about earned time credits or prerelease custody), or whether prisoners may also pursue such challenges through civil-rights actions. The split affects the procedural paths available to thousands of federal prisoners.

positions.label: Habeas is exclusive for challenges affecting duration/execution
positions.summary: Holds that when a prisoner's challenge to BOP decisions would affect the duration or execution of the sentence — including challenges to time credit calculations and prerelease custody — habeas corpus is the exclusive federal remedy.

positions.label: Civil-rights actions may be available for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement that do not directly challenge the fact or duration of imprisonment may be brought via civil-rights actions rather than habeas corpus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment attorney's fees order is governed by the civil 30-day deadline or the criminal 14-day deadline under the Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees in a criminal case is a civil or criminal matter for purposes of determining the appeal deadline. The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies because the motion is ancillary to the criminal case, while a minority of circuits apply the criminal deadline.

positions.label: Civil appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies.

positions.label: Criminal appeal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that because the Hyde Amendment motion arises in a criminal case, the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) governs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that orders denying motions to seal medical records qualify for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order' that would be irreparably lost without immediate review. Other circuits have taken varying approaches to whether sealing orders are immediately appealable, creating uncertainty about interlocutory appellate jurisdiction.

positions.label: Immediately appealable under collateral order doctrine
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable because maintaining medical privacy is a 'high order' value that would be irrevocably lost without immediate review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable because the party can seek adequate relief after final judgment, including sealing on remand or pursuing mandamus.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's property belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor when a Chapter 13 case is converted to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, while other circuits have held it belongs to the debtor, creating a circuit split that affects debtors' incentives to convert cases.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad definition of 'property of the estate' in § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition appreciation belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's purpose of protecting debtors who convert in good faith.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether RLUIPA permits suits for money damages against prison officials in their individual capacities. Some circuits allow such suits while others hold that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages, raising questions about the scope of Congressional spending power to impose personal liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA allows individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA authorizes suits for money damages against state prison officials in their individual capacities, as the statute's text is broad enough to encompass such claims.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Landor v. Louisiana Dep't of Corrections

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and Spending Clause legislation cannot impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under federal civil rights law?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to resolve disagreement among circuits over the standards for discrimination claims against hospitality and business operators, including questions about liability and available remedies. The Second Circuit's approach was deemed sufficiently unsettled to warrant review.

positions.label: Broader liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that broader standards apply to discrimination claims against business establishments, potentially allowing for more expansive remedies.

positions.label: Narrower liability standards
positions.summary: Holds that narrower standards govern such claims, limiting the scope of liability and available remedies for discrimination in public accommodations.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
